dx: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome with small cell lung cancer
case: A 62-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair. He also reports a dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. He has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years. Physical examination shows symmetric weakness of the hip and shoulder girdle muscles and mild bilateral ptosis. Patellar and biceps reflexes are absent at rest but can be elicited after 10 seconds of maximal voluntary contraction of the tested muscle. Sensation is intact. CT of the chest shows a large right hilar mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and bronchoscopic biopsy shows small cell carcinoma. Diagnosis: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome associated with small cell lung cancer.

questions.stem: Nerve conduction studies are performed. Which of the following electrodiagnostic findings is most likely in this patient?
options: Normal resting motor amplitude with a decrement at 3 Hz stimulation
Low resting motor amplitude that rises markedly after brief exercise
Reduced sensory nerve action potentials with slowed conduction velocity
Fibrillation potentials with large, long-duration motor units
approach: Notice the clues: proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, absent reflexes that return after exercise, and a smoker with small cell cancer.
Recall that this disorder reduces acetylcholine release, so each nerve impulse produces a small end plate potential.
Repeated activity builds up calcium in the nerve terminal and boosts release, so the response grows with exercise or fast stimulation.
questions.why: In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies block presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, so too little acetylcholine is released with each impulse. The resting compound muscle action potential is small. After brief maximal exercise or fast repetitive stimulation, calcium accumulates in the terminal and release improves, so the amplitude rises, often by more than 100%. Myasthenia gravis is the opposite pattern: a normal resting amplitude that falls with repeated stimulation, because the problem is fewer postsynaptic receptors.
whyNot: This is the classic pattern of myasthenia gravis. Release is normal, but receptors are lost, so the safety margin fails as release falls with repeated 3 Hz stimulation.
Correct.
Low sensory amplitudes and slowed conduction point to a peripheral neuropathy. Sensation is normal here, and Lambert-Eaton syndrome spares sensory nerves.
Fibrillations with large, long motor units are signs of denervation and reinnervation, as in motor neuron disease. They are not expected in a presynaptic junction disorder.

questions.stem: Serum testing shows antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following best classifies the immune mechanism of this patient's weakness?
options: Type III hypersensitivity from immune complexes deposited at end plates
Type IV hypersensitivity from CD8+ T cells attacking muscle fibers
Type I hypersensitivity from IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation
Type II hypersensitivity from IgG cross-reacting with a nerve antigen
approach: Identify the target: an antibody against a fixed membrane protein on the nerve terminal.
Link the source: small cell carcinoma cells are neuroendocrine and express the same calcium channel, so the immune response to the tumor cross-reacts with nerve.
An antibody against a cell-surface antigen that changes cell function is type II hypersensitivity.
questions.why: Small cell lung cancer cells express voltage-gated calcium channels. The immune response to the tumor makes IgG that also binds the channels on motor and autonomic nerve terminals. The antibodies cross-link and remove the channels, so less calcium enters and less acetylcholine is released. Antibody binding to a fixed cell-surface antigen is type II hypersensitivity, the same class as myasthenia gravis and the molecular mimicry of rheumatic fever.
whyNot: Type III injury comes from circulating immune complexes that lodge in vessel walls, as in SLE arthritis and glomerulonephritis. Here the antibody binds a fixed membrane protein.
Type IV injury by CD8+ T cells invading muscle fibers is the mechanism of polymyositis. Muscle fibers are normal in this disorder.
Type I reactions are immediate IgE-mediated allergic responses such as anaphylaxis and play no role in this weakness.
Correct.

topics: Paraneoplastic syndromes of small cell lung cancer

questions.stem: Six weeks later, he reports aching pain in both wrists and ankles. Examination shows clubbing of the fingers and warm, tender distal forearms and lower legs. Radiographs show smooth, symmetric periosteal new bone along the shafts of the distal radius, ulna, tibia, and fibula. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Paraneoplastic new bone formation linked to the lung tumor
Osteolytic metastases with a reactive periosteal bone response
PTH-related peptide causing subperiosteal bone resorption
Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in the joints
approach: Group the findings: clubbing, symmetric periosteal new bone on long bone shafts, and joint pain.
Recognize this triad as hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy.
Recall that it is a paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer and is not caused by tumor in the bone.
questions.why: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy is the triad of digital clubbing, periosteal new bone along the diaphyses of long bones, and arthritis of nearby joints. It is a paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer, more often non-small cell types, but it can occur with any lung tumor. The new bone is laid down symmetrically, which separates it from focal metastases. The leading explanation is that growth factors such as VEGF and PDGF act on the distal limbs.
whyNot: Correct.
Metastases are usually focal and asymmetric, often in the axial skeleton, and appear as lytic or blastic lesions within bone rather than smooth symmetric periosteal layers.
PTH-related peptide is made mostly by squamous cell carcinoma and causes hypercalcemia. Subperiosteal resorption is a sign of hyperparathyroidism and removes bone rather than adding it.
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition causes chondrocalcinosis and pseudogout attacks, often in the knee or wrist, but does not produce clubbing or periosteal new bone.

questions.stem: Treatment with amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine), a blocker of voltage-gated potassium channels in the nerve terminal, improves his strength. Which of the following best explains this improvement?
options: Inhibited acetylcholinesterase prolongs acetylcholine in the cleft
Increased number of postsynaptic nicotinic receptors
Prolonged terminal depolarization increases calcium entry
Protection of SNARE proteins from proteolytic cleavage
approach: Trace the steps: the action potential depolarizes the terminal, voltage-gated calcium channels open, calcium triggers SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion, and acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors.
Locate the defect in this disease at calcium entry.
Blocking potassium channels slows repolarization, so the remaining calcium channels stay open longer.
questions.why: Potassium efflux repolarizes the nerve terminal after each action potential. When those channels are blocked, the terminal stays depolarized longer, and the calcium channels that survive the antibody attack stay open longer. More calcium enters, more vesicles fuse through the SNARE complex, and the end plate potential reaches threshold more often. This treats the exact step that fails in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot: This is how pyridostigmine works. It helps most in myasthenia gravis, where the problem is postsynaptic, and it is not how a potassium channel blocker acts.
Potassium channel blockers do not change receptor number. Receptor loss is the defect in myasthenia gravis, and here the receptors are normal.
Correct.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks vesicle fusion. That is the defect in botulism, and SNARE proteins are intact here.

case: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of lifelong exercise intolerance. Within a few minutes of intense exercise she develops muscle pain, stiffness, and fatigue. If she rests briefly and then resumes at a slower pace, she can continue with much less discomfort. Two days ago, after sprint drills, she had painful cramps and passed dark red-brown urine. Her parents are healthy and are first cousins. Physical examination today is normal. Serum creatine kinase is 8,400 U/L (reference 30 to 170). A forearm exercise test shows no rise in venous lactate, while venous ammonia rises. Genetic testing shows biallelic pathogenic variants in PYGM, the gene for muscle glycogen phosphorylase. Diagnosis: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V).

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her symptoms ease when she rests briefly and then continues exercising?
options: Lysosomal acid maltase begins degrading stored muscle glycogen
Debranching enzyme releases free glucose from muscle glycogen
Muscle uptake of blood glucose and free fatty acids increases
Muscle glucose-6-phosphatase releases glucose into the cytosol
approach: Identify the defect: muscle cannot break down its own glycogen.
Ask what other fuels muscle can use: glucose from the blood (supplied by the liver, whose phosphorylase is a different enzyme) and fatty acids.
After a few minutes, blood flow and fuel delivery rise, so muscle shifts to these outside fuels. This is the second wind.
questions.why: McArdle disease is an autosomal recessive deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase, so muscle cannot mobilize its glycogen at the start of intense exercise. After several minutes, exercising muscle receives more blood flow and takes up more glucose released by the liver and more free fatty acids from adipose tissue. With these outside fuels, she can continue, which is the second wind. The same block explains the flat lactate curve, the cramps, and myoglobinuria after intense exertion.
whyNot: Acid maltase is the lysosomal enzyme missing in Pompe disease. Its small lysosomal pathway cannot supply energy for exercise.
Debranching enzyme acts only after phosphorylase has shortened the outer chains, and it releases very little free glucose. It cannot bypass the missing phosphorylase.
Correct.
Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, which is why muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose. This enzyme is found in liver and kidney.

topics: McArdle disease and the second wind

questions.stem: During one of her cramps, needle electromyography of the contracted muscle is electrically silent. The cramp is attributed to energy failure in the fibers. Which step in the contraction cycle most directly fails when muscle ATP is depleted?
options: Release of myosin heads from actin after ATP binding
Release of ADP from myosin at the end of the stroke
Calcium binding to troponin C to expose sites on actin
Depolarization of T tubules that activates DHP receptors
approach: An electrically silent contraction means the muscle is stuck in a contracted state without new action potentials.
Walk through the cross-bridge cycle and find the step that needs a fresh ATP molecule.
ATP binding releases myosin from actin. Without ATP, heads stay attached, as in rigor mortis.
questions.why: In the cross-bridge cycle, ATP binding to the myosin head releases it from actin. Hydrolysis then cocks the head, the head binds actin, and phosphate release drives the power stroke. When ATP runs out, myosin stays bound to actin and the fiber cannot relax, which is the mechanism of rigor mortis. An electrically silent contracture in McArdle disease reflects this kind of energy failure, unlike an ordinary cramp, which shows electrical activity.
whyNot: Correct.
ADP release does not need new ATP. It happens at the end of the power stroke and leaves the head bound to actin, so it does not explain failure to relax.
Calcium binding to troponin C does not use ATP. It starts contraction but does not explain why fibers stay locked once ATP is gone.
T tubule depolarization is electrical. The electromyogram is silent, so no new depolarizations are driving this contraction.

questions.stem: A muscle biopsy is fixed while the fibers are in a contracted state, and electron microscopy shows shortened sarcomeres. Compared with a relaxed sarcomere, which of the following keeps the same length?
options: I band
H zone
Distance between Z lines
A band
approach: Recall the sliding filament model: thin filaments slide past thick filaments, and neither filament changes length.
The A band equals the length of the thick filaments, so it stays the same.
Bands that contain only one kind of filament (I band, H zone) shrink as overlap increases, and the Z lines move closer together.
questions.why: The A band is the full length of the thick myosin filaments, and thick filaments do not shorten. During contraction, thin filaments slide toward the M line, so the overlap grows. The I band (thin filaments only) and the H zone (thick filaments only) both shorten, and the Z lines are pulled closer, shortening the sarcomere.
whyNot: The I band contains only thin filaments and shortens as they slide further into the A band.
The H zone contains only thick filaments and narrows, and can disappear, as thin filaments slide toward the M line.
The Z line to Z line distance is the sarcomere length itself, which shortens with contraction.
Correct.

questions.stem: She notes that she can perform a single 5-second maximal jump without any symptoms. Which of the following energy sources mainly supports this brief effort?
options: Anaerobic breakdown of muscle glycogen to lactate
Phosphocreatine transfer of phosphate to ADP
Oxidation of free fatty acids in mitochondria
Oxidation of ketone bodies released by the liver
approach: Match exercise duration to fuel: the first seconds use stored ATP and phosphocreatine, the next minute or so relies on anaerobic glycolysis, and longer work uses oxidative metabolism.
Her glycogen breakdown is blocked, yet a 5-second effort is normal.
That points to the phosphocreatine system, which does not need glycogen.
questions.why: In the first several seconds of maximal effort, muscle regenerates ATP from phosphocreatine through creatine kinase, which transfers phosphate to ADP. This system does not depend on glycogen, so it works normally in McArdle disease. Symptoms appear when the effort lasts long enough to need anaerobic glycolysis from muscle glycogen, the pathway she cannot start.
whyNot: Anaerobic glycolysis from muscle glycogen powers efforts lasting from several seconds to about 2 minutes. It is the pathway blocked in her disease.
Correct.
Fatty acid oxidation is slow to start and supports prolonged, lower-intensity work, not a single maximal burst.
Ketone bodies are used mainly during fasting by heart, muscle, and brain. They are too slow and too scarce to fuel a 5-second maximal effort.

case: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after finishing a 5-hour hike during which he ate nothing. He has diffuse muscle pain, weakness, and dark brown urine. He had two similar episodes, one after a long bicycle ride and one during a febrile illness. He can sprint without symptoms. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Thigh and calf muscles are tender. Serum studies show creatine kinase 62,000 U/L (reference 30 to 200), potassium 6.1 mEq/L (3.5 to 5.0), and creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, and microscopy shows 0 to 2 red blood cells per high-power field. Genetic testing shows biallelic CPT2 variants. Diagnosis: carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency with exertional rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following steps of fatty acid metabolism is deficient in this patient?
options: Transfer of long-chain acyl groups from CoA to carnitine
Activation of long-chain fatty acids to acyl-CoA in the cytosol
Dehydrogenation of medium-chain acyl-CoA in the matrix
Return of acyl groups from carnitine to CoA in the matrix
approach: Recall the carnitine shuttle: CPT I on the outer mitochondrial membrane moves long-chain acyl groups onto carnitine, a translocase carries acylcarnitine across the inner membrane, and CPT II on the inner membrane puts the acyl group back onto CoA.
Place CPT II at the last step, inside the matrix.
Link the defect to his triggers: prolonged exercise and fasting, when muscle depends most on long-chain fatty acid oxidation.
questions.why: CPT II sits on the matrix side of the inner mitochondrial membrane and converts long-chain acylcarnitine back to acyl-CoA so beta-oxidation can begin. When it is deficient, long-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidized. At rest and during short bursts, muscle runs on glucose and glycogen, so he is well. During prolonged exercise, fasting, cold, or fever, muscle relies on fatty acids, energy fails, and fibers break down.
whyNot: This is the CPT I reaction on the outer membrane. CPT I deficiency mainly affects the liver and causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia, and his gene test points to CPT II.
Acyl-CoA synthetase activates fatty acids in the cytosol before the shuttle. It is upstream of the defect.
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MCAD) causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia, mainly in infants, and is a beta-oxidation defect after the shuttle.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the rise in his serum creatinine?
options: Immune complex deposition in glomerular capillaries
Heme pigment toxicity and casts in renal tubules
Hemoglobin released by intravascular hemolysis
Interstitial nephritis from a drug hypersensitivity
approach: Read the urine: dipstick positive for blood but almost no red cells means a free heme pigment.
With a very high creatine kinase, the pigment is myoglobin from muscle breakdown.
Myoglobin filtered by the kidney injures tubules and forms casts, causing acute kidney injury.
questions.why: In rhabdomyolysis, injured muscle releases potassium, creatine kinase, and myoglobin. Myoglobin is small enough to be filtered. In the tubules its heme causes oxidant injury, and it precipitates into casts, especially in acidic, concentrated urine, while volume depletion lowers renal blood flow. The dipstick detects heme, so it reads positive for blood even though few red cells are seen. Hyperkalemia comes from release of intracellular potassium and worsens as kidney function falls.
whyNot: Immune complex glomerulonephritis causes hematuria with red cells and red cell casts, not a heme-positive urine with no red cells.
Correct.
Hemolysis also gives a heme-positive urine with few red cells, but it would not raise creatine kinase to 62,000 U/L. The muscle pain and tenderness point to myoglobin.

Drug-induced interstitial nephritis follows a new medication and often brings fever, rash, and white cells in the urine. Nothing in his history points to a drug, and the very high creatine kinase points to muscle breakdown.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of skeletal muscle fibers best explains why long, moderate-intensity exercise triggers his episodes while sprinting does not?
options: Type II fibers store glycogen that powers hours of steady work
Type I fibers have low myoglobin and few mitochondria
Type I fibers rely on fatty acid oxidation for steady work
Type II fibers are recruited first during low-intensity work
approach: Recall the two fiber types: type I are slow, red, oxidative, and fatigue resistant; type II are fast, glycolytic, and fatigable.
Long steady exercise mainly uses type I fibers, which burn fatty acids in their many mitochondria.
His defect blocks long-chain fatty acid oxidation, so the fibers doing endurance work run short of energy.
questions.why: Type I fibers are slow, red, and rich in mitochondria and myoglobin. They resist fatigue because they generate ATP oxidatively, and during prolonged exercise much of that fuel is fatty acids. Small motor units with type I fibers are recruited first, so they carry most of the load in long, moderate work. When CPT II is missing, these fibers cannot use their main sustained fuel. Sprinting relies on type II fibers powered by phosphocreatine and glycolysis, which are unaffected.
whyNot: Type II fibers do store glycogen, but they use it for short, intense bursts and fatigue quickly. They do not power hours of steady work.
Type I fibers are red because they are rich in myoglobin, and they have many mitochondria. This description is reversed.
Correct.
By the size principle, small motor units with type I fibers are recruited first. Type II units are added as force demands rise.

topics: Type I and type II muscle fibers

questions.stem: His sprints are powered largely by anaerobic glycolysis, and the lactate produced is carried to the liver. Which of the following describes what the liver does with this lactate and the net energy cost of the cycle?
options: Converts it to glucose, with a net cost of 4 ATP per glucose
Converts it to glucose, with a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose
Converts it to ketone bodies, with a net gain of 2 ATP
Converts it to alanine, with a net cost of 2 ATP
approach: Name the cycle: muscle lactate goes to the liver, is made into glucose, and glucose returns to muscle. This is the Cori cycle.
Count ATP: glycolysis in muscle yields 2 ATP per glucose, and gluconeogenesis from 2 lactate uses 6 high-energy phosphates.
The difference is a net cost of 4 ATP, paid by the liver.
questions.why: In the Cori cycle, lactate from anaerobic glycolysis travels to the liver, is oxidized to pyruvate, and is rebuilt into glucose by gluconeogenesis. The glucose returns to muscle. Muscle gains 2 ATP per glucose, but the liver spends 6 ATP equivalents to make one glucose from 2 lactate, so the cycle costs 4 ATP overall. The liver can afford this because it burns fatty acids for energy, and the cycle lets muscle keep working anaerobically.
whyNot: Correct.
Glucose is the right product, but the cycle costs energy. Gluconeogenesis uses more ATP than glycolysis yields.
Ketone bodies are made from acetyl-CoA during fat oxidation, not from lactate, and their synthesis does not yield ATP in this way.
Alanine carries amino groups from muscle to the liver in the glucose-alanine cycle. The liver converts alanine to glucose, not lactate to alanine.

case: A 17-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of 2 years of sudden jerking movements of his arms, unsteady gait, and fatigue and weakness with exertion. Six months ago he had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. His mother has bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and a maternal uncle had seizures and died at the age of 34 years. Physical examination shows multifocal myoclonus, gait ataxia, and mild proximal weakness. Serum lactate at rest is 4.8 mmol/L (reference 0.5 to 2.2). Gomori trichrome stain of a quadriceps biopsy shows ragged red fibers. Genetic testing of muscle shows the m.8344A>G variant in the mitochondrial tRNA-lysine gene in 85% of mitochondrial DNA copies. Diagnosis: myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers (MERRF).

questions.stem: His 20-year-old sister carries the same variant but has only mild exercise intolerance. Which of the following best explains the difference in severity between the siblings?
options: Different proportions of mutant mitochondrial DNA in their tissues
Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat in the more severely affected child
Random inactivation of the X chromosome carrying the variant
Genomic imprinting that silences the maternal copy of the gene
approach: Note the pattern: the variant is in mitochondrial DNA and passes through the mother to all her children.
Each cell holds many mitochondrial genomes, some normal and some mutant. This mix is heteroplasmy.
The proportion of mutant copies varies between siblings and between tissues, and disease appears when it crosses a threshold.
questions.why: Mitochondria come from the egg, so a mitochondrial DNA variant passes from a mother to all her children, while fathers do not transmit it. Each cell contains hundreds to thousands of mitochondrial genomes. When mutant and normal copies coexist (heteroplasmy), they are distributed randomly at cell division and into each egg. A sibling with a high mutant load in brain and muscle is severely affected, while one with a lower load may have mild or no symptoms. Ragged red fibers are muscle fibers packed with abnormal mitochondria that stain red under the sarcolemma on Gomori trichrome.
whyNot: Correct.

Trinucleotide repeat expansion explains anticipation in disorders such as myotonic dystrophy and Huntington disease. It is a nuclear gene mechanism and does not apply to a mitochondrial point variant.
X inactivation explains variable expression in females with X-linked disorders. Mitochondrial genes are not on the X chromosome.
Imprinting silences one parental copy of certain nuclear genes, as in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. Mitochondrial DNA is not imprinted.

questions.stem: His muscle fibers produce too little ATP, which slows the cross-bridge cycle. In a normal cycle, which of the following events directly produces the power stroke?
options: Binding of ATP to the myosin head
Hydrolysis of ATP by the myosin head
Release of inorganic phosphate from myosin
Detachment of the myosin head from the actin filament
approach: List the cycle in order: ATP binds and myosin detaches, ATP is hydrolyzed and the head is cocked, the head binds actin, phosphate is released and the power stroke occurs, then ADP leaves.
Separate the step that stores energy (hydrolysis cocks the head) from the step that uses it (phosphate release).
The power stroke follows phosphate release.
questions.why: Hydrolysis of ATP stores energy in the myosin head by cocking it into a high-energy position while ADP and phosphate remain bound. When the cocked head binds actin, release of inorganic phosphate triggers the power stroke, which pulls the thin filament toward the M line. ADP is released at the end of the stroke, leaving the head tightly bound until a new ATP arrives. Low ATP supply in mitochondrial myopathy limits how fast this cycle can repeat, causing early fatigue.
whyNot: ATP binding releases the head from actin. It ends one cycle and does not generate force.
Hydrolysis cocks the head and stores energy, but the head is not yet bound to actin, so no force is produced.
Correct.
Detachment follows ATP binding and allows the head to reset. It does not move the thin filament.

questions.stem: A supervised endurance training program is recommended. In healthy skeletal muscle, which of the following adaptations does sustained endurance training most characteristically produce?
options: Hypertrophy of type II fibers with more myofibrils
More mitochondria and capillaries in trained fibers
Greater phosphocreatine stores in type II muscle fibers
Conversion of type I fibers into type II fibers
approach: Separate training types: endurance training improves oxidative capacity, and resistance training enlarges fibers.
Oxidative capacity depends on mitochondria and on oxygen delivery through capillaries.
Pick the option that increases both.
questions.why: Endurance training increases the number and size of mitochondria, the amount of oxidative enzymes, and capillary density around muscle fibers. These changes raise oxidative capacity and fatigue resistance without much change in fiber size. Resistance training, by contrast, mainly causes hypertrophy of type II fibers by adding myofibrils. In mitochondrial myopathy, carefully supervised endurance training is used to build oxidative capacity in the fibers that remain.
whyNot: Type II fiber hypertrophy is the main adaptation to resistance training, not endurance training.
Correct.
Phosphocreatine supports brief maximal efforts. Endurance training does not mainly work by enlarging this short-term store.
Training does not convert type I fibers to type II. Endurance training tends to shift fibers toward more oxidative properties.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most support a myopathic rather than a neurogenic cause of his weakness?
options: Fiber type grouping on ATPase staining
Fasciculations in the tongue and thighs
Grouped atrophy of angular muscle fibers
Proximal weakness with elevated serum CK
approach: Neurogenic disease damages the motor neuron or axon, so whole motor units lose their nerve supply.
Denervation leads to fasciculations, groups of atrophic fibers, and fiber type grouping after reinnervation.
Myopathic disease damages the fibers themselves, so weakness is proximal and the leaking fibers raise creatine kinase.
questions.why: When a muscle fiber is damaged, creatine kinase leaks into the blood, and the large proximal muscles weaken first. This is the myopathic pattern, which fits a mitochondrial myopathy. Neurogenic disease, such as spinal muscular atrophy from SMN1 deletion, denervates whole motor units. Denervated fibers shrink in groups, surviving neurons reinnervate neighboring fibers and convert them to one type (fiber type grouping), and unstable motor units produce fasciculations.
whyNot: Fiber type grouping forms when surviving motor neurons reinnervate denervated fibers and convert them to their own type. It is a neurogenic sign.
Fasciculations are spontaneous firing of whole motor units and point to lower motor neuron disease.
Grouped atrophy of small angular fibers means a whole motor unit lost its nerve. It is a neurogenic sign.
Correct.

case: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 days after she felt a sudden pain in her lower back while lifting a heavy box. The pain now radiates down the back of her left thigh and the lateral side of her leg to the top of her foot and big toe. Coughing worsens the pain. A straight-leg raise on the left reproduces the leg pain at 40 degrees. Neurologic examination shows weak extension of the left big toe and weak ankle dorsiflexion, with decreased sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the first web space. Patellar and Achilles reflexes are normal and symmetric. MRI of the lumbar spine shows a left posterolateral disc herniation at the L4-L5 level. Diagnosis: L4-L5 intervertebral disc herniation.

questions.stem: Which of the following nerve roots is most likely compressed by this herniation?
options: L3
L4
L5
S1
approach: Recall that a lumbar root exits below the pedicle of its own vertebra, so the L4 root leaves through the L4-L5 foramen above the disc.
A posterolateral herniation bulges into the lateral recess and hits the root traveling down to exit at the next level.
At L4-L5 that root is L5, which fits weak big toe extension, weak dorsiflexion, numbness of the foot dorsum, and normal reflexes.
questions.why: With age, the nucleus pulposus dries out and the annulus fibrosus develops tears. The nucleus usually herniates posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is thinnest. In the lumbar spine, the root named for the upper vertebra has already exited above the disc, so a posterolateral L4-L5 herniation compresses the L5 root. L5 controls big toe extension and dorsiflexion and supplies skin on the dorsum of the foot, and it has no major reflex.
whyNot: L3 compression causes anterior thigh pain and weak knee extension and hip flexion. It would come from an L2-L3 herniation or a far lateral herniation at L3-L4.
L4 exits above the L4-L5 disc and is spared by a typical posterolateral herniation. Its compression would weaken knee extension and reduce the patellar reflex.
Correct.
S1 is compressed by an L5-S1 herniation. It weakens plantarflexion, reduces the Achilles reflex, and causes numbness of the lateral foot.

topics: Lumbar disc herniation and root level

questions.stem: If the herniation had occurred one level lower, at L5-S1, which reflex would most likely be reduced, and which afferent fibers carry that reflex?
options: Achilles reflex, carried by Ia afferents from muscle spindles
Patellar reflex, carried by Ia afferents from muscle spindles
Achilles reflex, carried by Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs
Patellar reflex, carried by Ib afferents from Golgi tendon organs
approach: An L5-S1 posterolateral herniation compresses the S1 root.
Match reflexes to roots: patellar is L4, Achilles is S1.
A tendon tap stretches the muscle, which activates spindle Ia afferents, so the stretch reflex runs through Ia fibers.
questions.why: Tapping the Achilles tendon briefly stretches the gastrocnemius and soleus. Muscle spindles sense the stretch and fire Ia afferents that synapse directly on alpha motor neurons, mostly at S1, causing plantarflexion. An S1 root lesion interrupts this arc and reduces the reflex. Golgi tendon organs sense tension, signal through Ib afferents, and inhibit the same muscle; they do not drive the stretch reflex.
whyNot: Correct.
The patellar reflex runs through L4 and would be affected by an L3-L4 lesion or a far lateral L4-L5 herniation, not an L5-S1 herniation.
The level is right, but Golgi tendon organs and Ib afferents sense tension and inhibit the muscle. The tendon jerk is a spindle Ia reflex.
Both parts are wrong: the patellar reflex is L4, and tendon reflexes use spindle Ia afferents, not Ib fibers.

topics: Muscle spindle versus Golgi tendon organ

questions.stem: Her physician must distinguish this L5 radiculopathy from a common fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck. Which of the following findings would best support the radiculopathy?
options: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and toe extension
Weakness of foot eversion against resistance
Reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot
Contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance
approach: Both lesions can cause foot drop, weak eversion, and numbness of the foot dorsum, so these do not separate them.
The L5 root also feeds nerves that the common fibular nerve does not carry, such as the superior gluteal nerve to gluteus medius and minimus.
Weak hip abduction shows as a Trendelenburg sign, with the pelvis dropping on the side opposite the weak muscle.
questions.why: The common fibular nerve supplies the anterior and lateral leg compartments and the skin of the dorsum of the foot, so its injury causes foot drop, weak eversion, and dorsal foot numbness. An L5 root lesion causes the same findings but also weakens L5 muscles supplied by other nerves. The superior gluteal nerve (L4 to S1) innervates gluteus medius and minimus, which hold the pelvis level during single-leg stance. Weakness of these muscles lets the pelvis drop on the opposite side, which places the lesion above the fibular neck.
whyNot: Weak dorsiflexion occurs with both lesions because the deep fibular nerve supplies tibialis anterior, which receives L4 and L5 fibers.
Weak eversion occurs with both lesions because the superficial fibular nerve supplies the fibularis muscles, which receive L5 and S1 fibers.
Numbness of the foot dorsum occurs with both lesions because the superficial fibular nerve carries this L5 skin area.
Correct.

topics: Root lesion versus peripheral nerve lesion

questions.stem: The herniated material passed through a radial tear in the annulus fibrosus. Which collagen types predominate in the outer annulus fibrosus and in the nucleus pulposus, respectively?
options: Type II and type I
Type I and type II
Type III and type II
Type I and type IV
approach: The outer annulus fibrosus is fibrocartilage built to resist tension, like tendon and ligament.
Tension-resisting tissues use type I collagen.
The nucleus pulposus is a hydrated gel that resists compression, like hyaline cartilage, and uses type II collagen.
questions.why: The outer annulus fibrosus is made of concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage that resist tension, and its main collagen is type I, as in tendon, ligament, and bone. The nucleus pulposus is a gel rich in proteoglycans with a fine network of type II collagen, the type found in hyaline cartilage. As the disc ages, the nucleus loses proteoglycans and water, and the annulus develops tears through which the nucleus can herniate.
whyNot: This reverses the two tissues. Type II collagen is the main collagen of the nucleus, not the outer annulus.
Correct.
Type III collagen forms reticular fibers and is prominent in vessels and early granulation tissue. It is not the main collagen of the annulus.
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes. It is not the main collagen of the nucleus pulposus.

dx: Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis with anterior uveitis
case: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 10-week history of swelling of her right knee and a limp that is worst in the morning. She has had no fever or rash. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F). Physical examination shows a warm right knee with a large effusion and a mild flexion contracture, and a swollen left ankle. No other joints are involved. Laboratory studies show a positive antinuclear antibody at a titer of 1:320, negative rheumatoid factor, a normal leukocyte count, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 28 mm/h (reference 0 to 20). Slit-lamp examination shows inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber of the right eye, although the eye is not red or painful. Diagnosis: oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis with anterior uveitis.

questions.stem: Her parents ask why she needs slit-lamp eye examinations every few months for several years. Which of the following features of this condition best explains this recommendation?
options: Uveitis usually begins only after the arthritis remits
Uveitis is usually painful but responds to topical lubricants
Uveitis is often silent until it damages vision
Uveitis occurs mainly in the systemic form of the disease
approach: Identify the subtype: arthritis in 4 or fewer joints for more than 6 weeks in a young ANA-positive girl is oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Recall that this subtype carries the highest risk of chronic anterior uveitis, especially when ANA is positive.
The uveitis usually causes no redness or pain, so only regular slit-lamp screening finds it before damage occurs.
questions.why: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is arthritis that starts before age 16 and lasts at least 6 weeks with no other cause. The oligoarticular form affects 4 or fewer joints, often the knee, and is most common in young girls. ANA positivity marks a high risk of chronic anterior uveitis, which is typically silent, with no redness or pain. Untreated, it can cause cataract, band keratopathy, glaucoma, and vision loss, so children are screened regularly with slit-lamp examination.
whyNot: Uveitis can appear before, with, or after the arthritis, and it can stay active when the joints are quiet. Its timing does not depend on remission.
The uveitis of oligoarticular disease is usually painless, and it needs anti-inflammatory treatment, not lubricants.
Correct.
Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis presents with daily spiking fever and a salmon-colored rash, and uveitis is uncommon in that form. The oligoarticular ANA-positive form has the highest risk.

questions.stem: At age 9 years, she develops pain in front of her right ear when chewing and a click when opening her mouth. MRI shows anterior displacement of the articular disc of the right temporomandibular joint. Which of the following nerves carries most of the pain sensation from this joint?
options: Chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve
Great auricular nerve from C2 and C3
Buccal branch of the facial nerve
Auriculotemporal branch of CN V3
approach: Recognize the temporomandibular joint as a synovial joint with an articular disc that allows hinge and gliding motion.
Apply Hilton law: the nerve to the muscles that move a joint also supplies the joint. The muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
The auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of CN V3 supply the joint capsule.
questions.why: The temporomandibular joint lies between the mandibular condyle and the temporal bone, with an articular disc dividing it into upper (gliding) and lower (hinge) compartments. When the disc slips forward, the condyle snaps back under it during opening, causing a click and pain. Sensation from the joint comes mainly from the auriculotemporal nerve, with help from the masseteric nerve, both branches of CN V3. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis often involves this joint and can disturb mandibular growth.
whyNot: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands. It does not supply the joint.
The great auricular nerve supplies skin over the parotid gland and earlobe, not the joint capsule.
The buccal branch of the facial nerve is motor to buccinator and muscles of the upper lip. It carries no joint sensation.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 35-year-old mother has had 4 months of symmetric pain and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands, with 2 hours of morning stiffness. Which of the following antibodies is most specific for the mother's most likely disease?
options: Anti-CCP antibody
Anti-dsDNA antibody
Anticentromere antibody
Anti-Jo-1 antibody
approach: Symmetric small joint arthritis of the hands with long morning stiffness in an adult suggests rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatoid factor is sensitive but not specific.
Antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptides are the most specific marker.
questions.why: Rheumatoid arthritis typically involves the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints symmetrically, with morning stiffness lasting more than an hour. Anti-CCP antibodies recognize citrullinated proteins and are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis. They can appear years before symptoms and predict more erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor is also common in rheumatoid arthritis but appears in many other conditions.
whyNot: Correct.
Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE, where arthritis is usually nonerosive and comes with rash, serositis, cytopenias, or nephritis.
Anticentromere antibodies mark limited systemic sclerosis, with Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias.
Anti-Jo-1 is a myositis antibody linked to interstitial lung disease, mechanic's hands, and arthritis in antisynthetase syndrome, with proximal muscle weakness.

questions.stem: Radiographs of the mother's hands show marginal erosions at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which of the following mechanisms most directly produces these erosions?
options: Uric acid crystals activating the NLRP3 inflammasome
RANKL-driven osteoclasts at the edge of synovial pannus
Mechanical wear of cartilage with subchondral sclerosis
Anti-dsDNA immune complexes in synovial vessels
approach: In rheumatoid arthritis, CD4+ T cells reacting to citrullinated peptides (linked to HLA-DR4) drive synovial inflammation through TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.
The inflamed synovium grows into a pannus that spreads over cartilage and bone at the joint margins.
Synovial cells and T cells express RANKL, which activates osteoclasts that cut marginal erosions.
questions.why: In rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-DR4 associated CD4+ T cells respond to citrullinated proteins and activate macrophages and B cells. Cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 cause synovial hyperplasia and inflammation, forming a pannus of proliferating synovium and granulation tissue. Pannus releases enzymes that destroy cartilage, and RANKL from synovial fibroblasts and T cells activates osteoclasts. Bone is eroded first at the joint margins, where synovium touches bone not covered by cartilage.
whyNot: Uric acid crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in gout. Gout erosions have overhanging edges and occur near tophi, often in the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
Correct.
Mechanical wear with subchondral sclerosis and osteophytes describes osteoarthritis, which favors the distal interphalangeal joints and is not erosive in this way.
Immune complexes cause the arthritis of SLE, which is typically nonerosive. Anti-dsDNA is not part of rheumatoid arthritis.

case: An 11-year-old girl in Connecticut is brought to the physician because of intermittent swelling of her left knee over the past 2 months. Each episode lasts about a week, and the knee is only mildly painful. She can walk normally. Last summer she spent several weeks at a wooded camp in Wisconsin and had an expanding red rash on her thigh that faded without treatment. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Examination shows a large, mildly warm effusion of the left knee with full range of motion. Other joints are normal. Serum enzyme immunoassay for Borrelia burgdorferi is positive and confirmed by IgG immunoblot. Diagnosis: Lyme arthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how she most likely acquired this infection?
options: Bite of a nymphal Ixodes tick attached for 36 hours or more
Bite of an adult Dermacentor tick attached for a few minutes
Bite of a larval Ixodes tick that hatched already infected
Bite of a body louse, with its feces rubbed into the skin
approach: Identify the organism: Borrelia burgdorferi, a spirochete.
Recall the cycle: Ixodes larvae hatch uninfected and pick up the organism from white-footed mice, then molt into nymphs.
Nymphs are small, are active in late spring and summer, and must stay attached for about 36 hours or more before the spirochete is transmitted.
questions.why: Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in white-footed mice. Ixodes scapularis larvae hatch uninfected because the spirochete is rarely passed through the egg; they acquire it when feeding on infected mice. After molting, the nymph transmits the spirochete during its next blood meal. Spirochetes multiply in the tick gut and move to the salivary glands over a day or more, so transmission usually needs about 36 hours or more of attachment. Nymphs are tiny and often unnoticed, which is why many patients do not recall a bite.
whyNot: Correct.
Dermacentor ticks transmit Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii), not Lyme disease, and a few minutes of attachment is too short for Borrelia.
Ixodes larvae hatch uninfected because transovarial transmission of B. burgdorferi is rare. They acquire the spirochete by feeding on infected mice.
Body lice transmit Borrelia recurrentis (louse-borne relapsing fever) when crushed lice are rubbed into the skin, and also epidemic typhus. They do not transmit Lyme disease.

questions.stem: Arthrocentesis of the left knee yields cloudy yellow fluid. Analysis shows a leukocyte count of 24,000/mm3 (normal under 200/mm3) with 75% neutrophils, a negative Gram stain, and no crystals on polarized light microscopy. Which of the following best classifies this fluid?
options: Noninflammatory, as in osteoarthritis
Hemorrhagic, as in traumatic hemarthrosis
Inflammatory, as in rheumatoid arthritis
Septic, as in staphylococcal joint infection
approach: Use leukocyte count cutoffs: under 2,000/mm3 is noninflammatory, 2,000 to about 50,000/mm3 is inflammatory, and septic fluid is usually over 50,000/mm3 with mostly neutrophils.
Her count of 24,000/mm3 falls in the inflammatory range, and the Gram stain is negative.
No crystals means this is not gout or pseudogout. Inflammatory fluid fits Lyme arthritis.
questions.why: Synovial fluid is grouped by leukocyte count. Noninflammatory fluid (under 2,000/mm3) is seen in osteoarthritis and trauma. Inflammatory fluid (about 2,000 to 50,000/mm3) is seen in rheumatoid arthritis, crystal arthritis, reactive arthritis, and Lyme arthritis, which often has counts of 10,000 to 50,000/mm3. Septic fluid usually exceeds 50,000/mm3 with over 90% neutrophils and often a positive Gram stain or culture. The ranges overlap, so culture, crystal search, and the clinical picture are always used together.
whyNot: Noninflammatory fluid has fewer than 2,000 leukocytes/mm3 and is clear. Her count is far higher.
Hemorrhagic fluid is bloody and follows trauma or a bleeding disorder. Her fluid is cloudy yellow, not bloody.
Correct.
Septic fluid usually has more than 50,000 leukocytes/mm3 with over 90% neutrophils, and bacteria are often seen on Gram stain. Her count is lower, the stain is negative, and she is nearly afebrile.

topics: Approach to the hot swollen joint

questions.stem: Before the effusion was linked to Lyme disease, she was examined for a soccer injury of the knee. Which of the following findings would have indicated a tear of the anterior cruciate ligament?
options: Medial joint line opening with valgus stress at 30 degrees of flexion
Lateral joint opening with varus stress at 30 degrees of flexion
Posterior tibial translation with the knee flexed 90 degrees
Anterior tibial translation with the knee flexed 20 to 30 degrees
approach: Recall that the ACL runs from the anterior tibia to the lateral femoral condyle and stops the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.
A torn ACL lets the tibia translate anteriorly, which the Lachman test (20 to 30 degrees of flexion) and the anterior drawer test (90 degrees) detect.
Match the other tests: valgus stress for MCL, varus stress for LCL, posterior drawer for PCL.
questions.why: The anterior cruciate ligament attaches to the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and the medial side of the lateral femoral condyle. It resists anterior translation of the tibia on the femur. The Lachman test, done at 20 to 30 degrees of flexion, is the most sensitive bedside test for an ACL tear, and the anterior drawer test at 90 degrees checks the same motion. The MCL is fused to the medial meniscus, which is why the two are often injured together.
whyNot: Medial opening with valgus stress tests the medial collateral ligament, which resists valgus force.
Lateral opening with varus stress tests the lateral collateral ligament, which resists varus force.
Posterior translation at 90 degrees is a positive posterior drawer test, indicating a PCL tear.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two months later, her 34-year-old mother develops symmetric swelling and stiffness of the small joints of both hands. One week earlier, the mother's 5-year-old son had bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on his arms. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the mother's arthritis?
options: HLA-B27 associated reactive arthritis
Parvovirus B19 associated arthritis
Disseminated gonococcal arthritis
Early Lyme arthritis from a tick bite
approach: Identify the child's illness: slapped-cheek rash followed by a lacy rash is erythema infectiosum, caused by parvovirus B19.
Recall that adults, especially women, infected with parvovirus B19 often develop symmetric small joint arthritis.
Distinguish it from reactive arthritis and Lyme arthritis, which are asymmetric and favor large joints of the legs.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum in children. Adults, especially women, often have little or no rash but develop acute symmetric polyarthritis of the hands, wrists, and knees that resembles rheumatoid arthritis. The arthritis is immune-mediated and usually resolves within weeks. Rubella infection and, less often, rubella vaccination can cause a similar transient arthritis or arthralgia in adult women.
whyNot: Reactive arthritis follows enteric or chlamydial infection, is linked to HLA-B27, and is usually an asymmetric arthritis of the large joints of the legs.
Correct.
Disseminated gonococcal infection causes migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis, and pustular skin lesions, or a purulent monoarthritis. It does not follow a child's rash.
Lyme arthritis is a late finding that affects one or a few large joints, mainly the knee. It does not cause symmetric small joint arthritis after a child's rash.

dx: Adhesive capsulitis with Dupuytren contracture in diabetes
case: A 56-year-old woman with a 12-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 5-month history of pain and progressive stiffness of the right shoulder. She can no longer reach behind her back or brush her hair. She has had no injury. Her hemoglobin A1c is 8.9% (reference under 5.7). Examination shows marked loss of both active and passive external rotation and abduction of the right shoulder; strength is normal within the available range. In the left palm there is a firm nodule with a cord extending to the ring finger, which cannot be fully extended at the metacarpophalangeal joint. Radiographs of the right shoulder are normal. Diagnosis: adhesive capsulitis of the right shoulder and Dupuytren contracture of the left hand.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her shoulder cannot be moved passively by the examiner?
options: Full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon
Inflammation and fibrosis of the joint capsule
Calcium pyrophosphate deposits in the labrum
Denervation of the deltoid by axillary nerve injury
approach: Compare active and passive motion: muscle, tendon, or nerve problems reduce active motion, but the examiner can still move the arm passively.
When passive motion is also lost, something inside the joint or capsule is mechanically blocking movement.
With normal radiographs and diabetes, the best fit is a thickened, contracted capsule.
questions.why: Adhesive capsulitis is inflammation followed by fibrosis and contraction of the glenohumeral joint capsule. The capsule shrinks and loses its folds, so both active and passive motion are limited, especially external rotation and abduction. Radiographs are normal, which separates it from arthritis. Diabetes is a major risk factor, and the condition often coexists with other fibrosing hand disorders such as Dupuytren contracture.
whyNot: A rotator cuff tear weakens active abduction, but the examiner can usually move the arm passively through a full range.
Correct.
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition causes acute pseudogout or chronic arthropathy, with chondrocalcinosis often visible on radiographs. Her radiographs are normal.
Axillary nerve injury weakens deltoid abduction but does not stop passive movement. Her strength is also normal.

topics: Active versus passive range of motion

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the contracture of her left ring finger?
options: Synovial inflammation of the flexor tendon sheaths
Thickening of the A1 pulley over the flexor tendons
Fibrosis of the metacarpophalangeal joint capsule
Myofibroblast proliferation in the palmar fascia
approach: Find the location of the lesion: a palpable nodule and cord in the palm, superficial to the tendons.
That tissue is the palmar aponeurosis.
Contractile myofibroblasts in this fascia form the nodules and cords that pull the ring and little fingers into flexion.
questions.why: Dupuytren contracture is a fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia. Myofibroblasts, which contain smooth muscle actin, form nodules and then cords of dense collagen that shorten over time. The cords pull the ring and little fingers into flexion at the metacarpophalangeal and then the proximal interphalangeal joints. Risk factors include diabetes, family history, alcohol use, and smoking.
whyNot: Flexor tenosynovitis causes pain and swelling along the tendon sheath, as in rheumatoid arthritis or infection, without a fascial cord in the palm.
Thickening of the A1 pulley causes trigger finger, with catching or locking during finger flexion rather than a fixed palmar cord.
Capsular fibrosis of the joint itself is not the source of a palpable palmar cord.
Correct.

questions.stem: Two years later, she falls on her outstretched, abducted, externally rotated right arm and sustains an anterior dislocation of the glenohumeral joint. After reduction, which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Winging of the scapula with weak protraction of the arm
Wrist drop with numbness over the dorsum of the hand
Weak abduction with numbness of the lateral shoulder
Weak elbow flexion with numbness of the lateral forearm
approach: The glenohumeral joint has a shallow glenoid and depends on the rotator cuff and capsule for stability, so it dislocates easily, usually anteriorly and inferiorly.
The displaced humeral head stretches the axillary nerve as it winds around the surgical neck.
Predict loss of deltoid function (abduction from about 15 to 90 degrees) and numbness over the lateral shoulder.
questions.why: The glenoid fossa is shallow and covers only part of the humeral head, so stability comes mainly from the rotator cuff muscles and the capsule and labrum. The anterior-inferior capsule is weakest, so most dislocations are anterior. The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space and around the surgical neck of the humerus, where the displaced head can stretch it. Injury weakens the deltoid and teres minor and causes numbness over the lateral shoulder (the regimental badge area). Supraspinatus can still start abduction for the first 15 degrees.
whyNot: Scapular winging comes from long thoracic nerve injury, usually after surgery or trauma along the chest wall, not from anterior dislocation.
Wrist drop comes from radial nerve injury, typically at the spiral groove with a midshaft humeral fracture.
Correct.
Weak elbow flexion with lateral forearm numbness comes from musculocutaneous nerve injury, which is much less common with dislocation than axillary nerve injury.

questions.stem: The myofibroblasts in her palmar cords express alpha-smooth muscle actin and contract in a way that resembles smooth muscle. In smooth muscle, which of the following events directly allows myosin to begin cross-bridge cycling?
options: Phosphorylation of myosin light chains by their kinase
Binding of calcium to troponin C on thin filaments
Dephosphorylation of myosin light chains by a phosphatase
Rise in cGMP after nitric oxide enters the cell
approach: Recall that smooth muscle has no troponin, so regulation is on the myosin side.
Calcium binds calmodulin, and calcium-calmodulin activates myosin light chain kinase.
Phosphorylated myosin light chains allow cross-bridge cycling. The phosphatase reverses this and relaxes the cell.
questions.why: In smooth muscle, a rise in cytosolic calcium leads to calcium binding calmodulin. The calcium-calmodulin complex activates myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of myosin and allows cross-bridges to form and cycle. Myosin light chain phosphatase removes the phosphate and causes relaxation. If myosin is dephosphorylated while still attached, the cross-bridges cycle slowly and hold tension at low energy cost, which is the latch state.
whyNot: Correct.
Troponin C regulates skeletal and cardiac muscle. Smooth muscle lacks troponin.
Myosin light chain phosphatase removes the phosphate and causes relaxation, not contraction.
Nitric oxide raises cGMP, which activates protein kinase G and favors relaxation by lowering calcium and activating the phosphatase.

dx: Renal osteodystrophy in chronic kidney disease
case: A 67-year-old man with chronic kidney disease from diabetic nephropathy comes to the physician because of aching pain in his hips, lower back, and ribs for 6 months. He also has difficulty rising from a chair. He is not yet on dialysis. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 14 mL/min/1.73 m2 (reference over 90). Serum studies show calcium 8.1 mg/dL (reference 8.5 to 10.5), phosphate 6.8 mg/dL (2.5 to 4.5), parathyroid hormone 640 pg/mL (10 to 65), alkaline phosphatase 310 U/L (40 to 130), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 34 ng/mL (30 to 100), and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 9 pg/mL (18 to 72). Radiographs of the hands show subperiosteal bone resorption along the radial sides of the middle phalanges. Diagnosis: renal osteodystrophy with secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his elevated parathyroid hormone concentration?
options: Autonomous secretion by a parathyroid adenoma
Ectopic PTH-related peptide from a carcinoma
Excess calcitriol from extrarenal hydroxylase
Phosphate retention and calcitriol deficiency
approach: Look at the direction of each value: calcium is low, phosphate is high, PTH is high, and calcitriol is low.
High PTH with low calcium means the parathyroids are responding appropriately, which is secondary hyperparathyroidism.
Failing kidneys retain phosphate and make less calcitriol, and both lower serum calcium and stimulate PTH.
questions.why: As kidney function falls, phosphate excretion drops and serum phosphate rises. High phosphate binds calcium and also stimulates the parathyroids directly. The diseased kidney makes less calcitriol, so intestinal calcium absorption falls, and FGF23 from osteocytes rises and further suppresses calcitriol. Low calcium, high phosphate, and low calcitriol all drive PTH up. Chronic high PTH increases bone turnover and resorption, causing osteitis fibrosa cystica with subperiosteal resorption, while low calcitriol impairs mineralization.
whyNot: A parathyroid adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism, with high calcium and low or normal phosphate. His calcium is low and phosphate is high.
PTH-related peptide causes hypercalcemia and suppresses native PTH. His PTH is high and his calcium is low.
Extrarenal calcitriol production, as in sarcoidosis, raises calcium and suppresses PTH. His calcitriol is low.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how parathyroid hormone increases osteoclast activity in his skeleton?
options: Induces osteoblast RANKL, activating osteoclast precursors
Binds receptors on osteoclasts to directly increase resorption
Raises osteoprotegerin secretion, which activates osteoclasts
Releases calcitonin, which stimulates osteoclast resorption
approach: Recall that PTH receptors are on osteoblasts and osteocytes, not osteoclasts.
PTH makes osteoblasts express RANKL and less osteoprotegerin.
RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and drives their maturation and activity, so PTH acts on osteoclasts indirectly.
questions.why: Osteoclasts do not have PTH receptors. PTH binds receptors on osteoblasts and osteocytes, which then increase RANKL and decrease osteoprotegerin. RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and, with M-CSF, drives them to fuse and resorb bone. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL and limits this process. PTH also increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, increases phosphate excretion, and activates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, although the last effect fails in advanced kidney disease.
whyNot: Correct.
This is a common misconception. Osteoclasts lack PTH receptors, so the effect is indirect through osteoblasts.
Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL and inhibits osteoclasts. PTH lowers it.
Calcitonin from thyroid C cells inhibits osteoclasts. PTH does not cause calcitonin release.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why his 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration is normal while his 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D concentration is low?
options: Reduced synthesis of vitamin D3 in sun-exposed skin
Reduced 25-hydroxylation of vitamin D in the liver
Reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney
Reduced intestinal absorption of dietary vitamin D
approach: Trace activation: 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin becomes vitamin D3 with UVB light, the liver adds a 25-hydroxyl group, and the kidney adds the 1-alpha-hydroxyl group.
A normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D means skin synthesis, intake, and liver conversion are adequate.
The block must be at the final renal step.
questions.why: Vitamin D3 is made in the skin when UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol, or it comes from the diet. The liver converts it to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the main circulating form, whose level reflects total vitamin D supply. The proximal tubule then adds a 1-alpha-hydroxyl group to form active calcitriol. In chronic kidney disease, loss of renal mass and high FGF23 reduce 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so calcitriol falls even when 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal.
whyNot: Reduced skin synthesis lowers the supply of vitamin D and would lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which is normal here.
Reduced hepatic 25-hydroxylation, as in severe liver disease, would lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Correct.
Poor intestinal absorption, as in fat malabsorption, reduces supply and would lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

questions.stem: His serum alkaline phosphatase is elevated because bone turnover is high. Which of the following best describes the bone cells that are the main source of this enzyme?
options: Multinucleated cells of monocyte and macrophage origin
Mesenchymal-derived cells that secrete osteoid
Mechanosensing cells within mineralized lacunae
Hypertrophic chondrocytes within a growth plate
approach: Recall that bone alkaline phosphatase is a marker of bone formation.
Bone formation is carried out by osteoblasts, which come from mesenchymal cells and secrete type I collagen osteoid.
In high-turnover bone disease, increased resorption is coupled with increased osteoblast activity, so alkaline phosphatase rises.
questions.why: Osteoblasts arise from mesenchymal stem cells. They secrete type I collagen osteoid and alkaline phosphatase, which helps mineralize the matrix by raising local phosphate. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, resorption and formation both speed up, so osteoblast activity and serum alkaline phosphatase rise. Osteoclasts, the multinucleated resorbing cells, come from the monocyte and macrophage lineage and use acid and cathepsin K in Howship lacunae.
whyNot: This describes osteoclasts, which resorb bone with acid and cathepsin K. They are a source of tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase, not alkaline phosphatase.
Correct.
This describes osteocytes, which sense mechanical load and secrete FGF23 and sclerostin. They are not the main source of serum alkaline phosphatase.
Growth plates are closed in adults. Hypertrophic chondrocytes are found only in growing bones.

dx: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis presenting as knee pain
case: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 6-week history of dull pain in his left knee and a limp. The pain is worse after sports. He recalls no injury. His body mass index is at the 98th percentile for age and sex. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). Examination of the left knee shows no swelling, tenderness, or instability. Passive flexion of the left hip produces obligatory external rotation, and internal rotation of the hip is markedly limited and painful. Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral radiographs of the pelvis show posterior and inferior displacement of the left femoral head relative to the femoral neck. Diagnosis: slipped capital femoral epiphysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient best distinguishes his disorder from Legg-Calve-Perthes disease?
options: Displacement of the femoral head at the physis
Limited and painful internal rotation of the hip
Hip disease presenting as pain in the knee
Limp without fever or a history of injury
approach: List what the two disorders share: a limp, hip or knee pain, loss of internal rotation, and no fever.

Recall what differs: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head in children about 4 to 8 years old, while this disorder is a slip of the epiphysis through the physis in an obese adolescent.
Pick the finding that reflects the slip itself: the femoral head displaced on the neck at the growth plate.
questions.why: In slipped capital femoral epiphysis, the femoral neck moves anteriorly and superiorly while the epiphysis stays in the acetabulum, so the head looks displaced posteriorly and inferiorly on radiographs. The slip happens through the weak hypertrophic zone of the physis during the growth spurt, and obesity adds shear force. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head, usually at about 4 to 8 years of age, and radiographs show a flattened or fragmented head that has not slipped. Developmental dysplasia of the hip is found in newborns with the Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of internal rotation is a sign of hip joint disease in general. It is also seen in Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, so it does not separate the two.
Both disorders can present as knee pain, because nerves to the hip also supply the knee. It does not separate the two.
Both disorders usually cause a limp without fever or a clear injury. Fever with refusal to bear weight would instead suggest septic arthritis.

topics: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis versus Legg-Calve-Perthes disease

questions.stem: Before hip radiographs were obtained, his knee pain was thought to come from a common adolescent knee disorder. Which of the following findings would have instead supported Osgood-Schlatter disease?
options: Anterior knee pain worsened by sitting with the knees bent
Knee locking with a loose fragment from the femoral condyle
Hip pain with limited internal rotation of the hip
Tender swelling over the tibial tubercle
approach: Recall that Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis where the patellar tendon pulls on the tibial tubercle apophysis.
It is common in active adolescents during growth spurts.
The key finding is a tender, sometimes enlarged, tibial tubercle.
questions.why: In Osgood-Schlatter disease, repeated pull of the quadriceps through the patellar tendon irritates the tibial tubercle apophysis in growing adolescents. Running and jumping worsen the pain, and the tubercle is tender and often prominent. Chondromalacia patellae is softening of patellar cartilage with anterior knee pain, often worse after long sitting. Osteochondritis dissecans is separation of a fragment of subchondral bone and cartilage, often from the medial femoral condyle, which can cause locking.
whyNot: Anterior knee pain after long sitting with bent knees suggests chondromalacia patellae, which involves the patellar cartilage, not the tibial tubercle.
Locking with a loose fragment suggests osteochondritis dissecans, which separates subchondral bone and cartilage.
Limited hip internal rotation points to a hip disorder such as this patient's, not to Osgood-Schlatter disease.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why disease of his hip was felt as pain in the knee?
options: The superior and inferior gluteal nerves supply both joints
The obturator and femoral nerves supply both joints
The pudendal and genitofemoral nerves supply both joints
The lateral femoral cutaneous and saphenous nerves supply both joints
approach: Apply Hilton law: the nerves that supply the muscles moving a joint also supply that joint.
The femoral and obturator nerves send branches to the hip capsule and also to the knee.
Pain from the hip carried in these nerves can be perceived in the knee, their shared territory.
questions.why: Hilton law states that a nerve supplying the muscles acting on a joint also supplies the joint and the skin over it. The hip capsule receives branches from the femoral and obturator nerves, and both nerves also send articular branches to the knee. Because the brain cannot always tell which end of the nerve's territory the signal came from, hip pain is often felt in the thigh or knee. This is why a child or adolescent with knee pain and a normal knee exam needs a hip exam.
whyNot: The gluteal nerves supply the gluteal muscles and do not supply the knee joint.
Correct.
The pudendal nerve supplies the perineum, and the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and skin of the upper anterior thigh. Neither supplies both joints.
These are cutaneous nerves to the skin of the thigh and medial leg. They do not carry pain from the hip joint.

questions.stem: After surgical fixation, he begins physical therapy with active knee extension exercises. As the quadriceps shortens, which of the following keeps its muscle spindles able to detect further stretch?
options: Ib afferent firing from Golgi tendon organs
Renshaw cell inhibition of alpha motor neurons
Gamma motor neuron activation of intrafusal fibers
Alpha motor neuron activation of extrafusal fibers
approach: Muscle spindles lie parallel to extrafusal fibers and sense stretch through Ia afferents.
When the muscle shortens, the spindle would go slack and stop firing.
Gamma motor neurons contract the ends of intrafusal fibers, taking up the slack so the spindle stays sensitive.
questions.why: Muscle spindles are made of intrafusal fibers lying in parallel with the main extrafusal fibers. When the muscle shortens, the spindle would go slack and its Ia afferents would fall silent. Gamma motor neurons fire along with alpha motor neurons (alpha-gamma coactivation), contracting the ends of the intrafusal fibers and keeping the central sensory region taut. This keeps the spindle able to signal length changes during movement.
whyNot: Golgi tendon organs lie in series with the muscle and sense tension through Ib afferents. They do not reset spindle sensitivity.
Renshaw cells provide recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons. They do not act on intrafusal fibers.
Correct.
Alpha motor neurons contract the extrafusal fibers, which shortens the muscle and unloads the spindle rather than keeping it taut.

topics: Muscle spindle and gamma motor neurons
